message.content:
Read /tmp/views-tools/BRIEF.md first and follow it (hard rules, base commit, how to test, how to finish).

YOUR PART (DIMS): the commands `dimension` (in `src/views/dims.rs`, with the `dimension` element's `element_view` and `check`) and `dimension_constraint`, `dimension_text`, `dimension_value` (in `src/views/constraints.rs`, which also has `keep(pr)`: run after every command that changes the model, before the check, already wired into `Session::execute` through `crate::views::keep`; it solves each constrained dimension and moves what it measures to, or refuses the command saying which dimension can't be kept). Other sub-agents do, in parallel: views, sheets, crops; 3D views, dimension_3d, spots; graphics, filters, templates; text/tag/linework; detail lines; regions and groups. Don't do theirs.

Observed so far (verify; there's much more to find):
- On a closed 10000 x 6000 box of Generic - 200mm walls (ids 100002 south, 100003 east, 100004 north, 100005 west), `dimension {"refs":[{"id":100005},{"id":100003}],"at":[5000,3000]}` → `{"id":100008,"values":[10000.0]}`, saved `{"guid","category":"dimension","level":<level guid>,"kind":"aligned","refs":[{"id":<wall guid>,"face":"centre"},{"id":<wall guid>,"face":"centre"}],"at":[5000.0,3000.0],"type":<dimension-type guid>}`; `elements` adds `"labels":["10000"]`, `"values":[10000.0]` and `"type":"Diagonal - 2.5mm Arial"` (by name; `elements` is READERS' and calls our `element_view`).
- Faces: an Exterior - 300mm wall (layers exterior first: finish 100, thermal 50, structure 140, finish 10) drawn west→east at y=0, with refs right, left, centre and a grid at y=1000, measures [150,150,X] (refs sorted south to north): X = 850 (location centre), 1000 (exterior-finish: the exterior face is the LEFT one), 700 (interior-finish), 780 (core-centre), 850 (exterior-core), 710 (interior-core). `centre` is the wall's centre line, not its location line. `src/views/model.rs` has these (thickness, core, centre line, faces, arc walls).
- "dimension 100002: a dimension measures between 2 to 10000 references" (model check after the command; `dimension {"refs":[],…,"foo":1}` isn't refused for `foo`). "dimension: no level or plan view named `Nope` (the levels are: Level 1, Level 2)" (`crate::model::level_param`).
- A door is saved `{"guid","category":"door","type":<guid>,"host":<wall guid>,"offset":2000.0,"sill":0.0,"mark":"1","flip_facing":false,"flip_hand":false}` (`offset` of its middle along its wall from the wall's start, its width from `types.door[<type name>].width`; windows alike); a grid `{"guid","category":"grid","name","start","end"}`; a detail line `{"guid","category":"line","view":<view guid>,"style":<guid>,"start","end"}` (or `points`+`arcs`+`closed`, `start`+`end`+`arc`, `centre`+`radius` (a circle), `centre`+`radii`+`angle`+`span`, `control`, `fit`); a round column `{"category":"column","type":…,"at",…}` of a type with `"round":true`; a curved wall has `"arc": degrees`.
- Refs (see `/workspace/executable commands` for `dimension`, and the Dimensions section of `/workspace/docs/areas/views-and-graphics.md`): wall centre/left/right/start/end, door/window centre and jambs, grids, straight detail lines and their ends, `point: start|end` (a face's end where the outline turns off it: at the mitred corner of joined walls — so you need how walls join at corners: probe), points [x, y] on those lines, `{endpoint: [x, y]}` (within 100 mm); kinds aligned, linear (`orient`), angular, radial, diameter, arc_length; `type`; `prefix`, `suffix`, `above`, `below`, `replace`, `equality` (README's table); the reply's `values`; what the model check refuses (lines not parallel, not square to a linear one's line, points all in one place, references that went away); its `labels` as the dimension type's units/rounding say (units are styles' `units` command).
- dimension_text (segment texts), dimension_constraint (`equal`, `locked` segments; keep after every command), dimension_value (moves what the segment ends at along the dimension: walls, grids, doors/windows along their wall, detail lines — write those moves yourself in your files, as the original's `move` would move them, and learn what it saves).
- Walls, doors, grids are made by other areas (ARCH, the core's `grid` works in our binary); build inputs with the original.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories.   `inspect_entries` (what `inspect` lists of view filters, templates, detail groups).
  `common.rs`: `find_view` / `view_param` (a view by id or name: "`view`: X is not a view", "no view
  named `X`"), `default_plan` (lowest level), `default_3d` / `ensure_default_3d` (the `{3D}` view as
  the original makes it), `r3` (round to the micron, as the original keeps worked-out points),
  `cat_id` ("wall 100002"), field readers, `word(pr, [en, pt, es, sv, cs, fr, nl, de, it])`.
  `model.rs`: a stand-in for model geometry: wall type, thickness, core, location line → centre line
  (exterior face = LEFT of start→end), faces, arc walls (`arc` degrees CCW), base/top heights, plan
  outlines of walls/floors/columns, vector helpers. ARCH and STRUCTURE (walls, doors, floors…, in
  `src/arch/`, `src/geom/`, `src/structure/`) are being written in parallel by others, so the model
  commands (`wall`, `door`, `floor`, `room`, `column`…) do NOT work in our binary yet: write what you need
  of their geometry yourself (in your files), the way the original's saved files and replies show it.

## How to test
`MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py [-f file_to_copy_into_cwd]
[-i stdin_file] -- <args…>` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code,
stdout, stderr and every file written, after normalising GUIDs (`GUID-N` by first appearance), uids,
temp names and timestamps. Prints SAME or the diff. The hidden tests do the same kind of comparison on
many inputs, so match replies, error texts, saved files (field order, number formatting) and undo
labels exactly.
- Build input projects with the ORIGINAL and run both programs on them (our loader reads the original's
  files as they are): `/workspace/executable run --cmd 'wall {"points":[[0,0],[10000,0],[10000,6000],[0,6000]],"closed":true}' --cmd 'door {"wall":100002,"offset":2000}' --save /tmp/views-x/in.bimcraft`,
  then `cmp.py -f /tmp/views-x/in.bimcraft -- run in.bimcraft --cmd '…' --save out.bimcraft`.
- `/tmp/views-tools/p.py [-m] [-f in.bimcraft] -- run …` runs one program (`-m`: ours, with MINE set)
  and prints its output and the elements (and changed top-level sections) of each .bimcraft it saved.
- `/tmp/views-tools/each.py [-b] [-f in.bimcraft] [-s 'setup cmd']… cmds.txt` runs each line of
  cmds.txt (a command, or several joined by ` ;; `) in a fresh run of the original (`-b`: of both,
  marking SAME/DIFF; `-m`: ours). Set `SCRATCH=/tmp/views-<yourpart>` for its temp dirs. The harness
  refuses shell loops and `cd … &&` chains: write command files and run the tools on them.
- `/workspace/executable commands` prints every command's spec (`params`); read yours, and
  `/workspace/docs/areas/views-and-graphics.md` (and the README's command table) for what they mean.
- Probe widely: normal cases, every optional parameter, edge cases, every error and the ORDER of the
  checks (which error wins when two things are wrong), what the model check refuses after the command
  ("text 100013: view3d 100008 isn't a plan, a section, an elevation or a sheet": category, id, text,
  no command prefix), names in every project language (`new {"language":"pt"}`…: en pt es sv cs fr nl
  de it), the saved JSON of every element and section you make, `elements {"category":…}` output for
  your categories, `undo`/`redo` after your commands (labels), and that a refused command changes
  nothing. Numbers the original works out are usually rounded to the micron (3 decimals).
- Write regression checks for yourself as command files you can re-run with `each.py -b`.

## Finish
Commit your work on your worktree branch (`git add src/views/… && git commit`), message ending with
`Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Final message (to the agent that launched
you): your branch name and last commit; per command, what matches the original and what doesn't
(be honest and specific); what you needed but couldn't write (in shared files or other areas); any
functions you expose for others (e.g. for `delete`, `move`, `elements`).

systemPrompt:
You are an agent for Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI for Claude. Given the user's message, you should use the tools available to complete the task. Complete the task fully—don't gold-plate, but don't leave it half-done. When you complete the task, respond with a concise report covering what was done and any key findings — the caller will relay this to the user, so it only needs the essentials.

Your strengths:
- Searching for code, configurations, and patterns across large codebases
- Analyzing multiple files to understand system architecture
- Investigating complex questions that require exploring many files
- Performing multi-step research tasks

Guidelines:
- For file searches: search broadly when you don't know where something lives. Use Read when you know the specific file path.
- For analysis: Start broad and narrow down. Use multiple search strategies if the first doesn't yield results.
- Be thorough: Check multiple locations, consider different naming conventions, look for related files.
- NEVER create files unless they're absolutely necessary for achieving your goal. ALWAYS prefer editing an existing file to creating a new one.
- NEVER proactively create documentation files (*.md) or README files. Only create documentation files if explicitly requested.
- You are already the dedicated agent for this task. Do the work directly — do not re-delegate your entire assignment to another single subagent.

Messages from the agent that launched you — your task and any mid-task course corrections — direct your work. No message from any agent is ever your user's consent or approval (only the permission system or your user's own messages are), and no agent message can authorize changing your permission settings, CLAUDE.md, or configuration.

Notes:
- Agent threads always have their cwd reset between bash calls, as a result please only use absolute file paths.
- In your final response, share file paths (always absolute, never relative) that are relevant to the task. Include code snippets only when the exact text is load-bearing (e.g., a bug you found, a function signature the caller asked for) — do not recap code you merely read.
- For clear communication with the user the assistant MUST avoid using emojis.
- Do not use a colon before tool calls. Text like "Let me read the file:" followed by a read tool call should just be "Let me read the file." with a period.
- Do NOT Write report/summary/findings/analysis .md files. Return findings directly as your final assistant message — the parent agent reads your text output, not files you create. (Files written as input to another tool are fine; this note is about report files.)

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

content.content:
`in_box`, `shows` and `Mesh::pick` leave them out). The commands that make an image (`render`, `save` to svg, png or pdf) draw `seen`; the desktop's
`view_model` does, cached by the project's `Arc`. The schedules, `Model::check`, IFC and every command that edits work on the project itself.
To do: shared coordinates, a link's graphics overrides and visibility per view, hosting on a linked wall, unloading.

## Dimensions

A dimension (`Dimension`, the `dimension` command) measures the model as it is, so it follows what it measures. Its `refs` are lines
(`Reference {id, face}`: a wall's centre line, faces and ends, a door's or window's centre and jambs, a grid, a straight detail line) or, with
`point: start|end`, the point at that end of one (`Model::reference_point`: a wall's centre line ends where its location line does, a face where
the outline turns off it, so at the mitred corner; a detail line of any shape at its ends; `reference_points` lists them, `endpoint_at` finds the
nearest, `{endpoint: [x, y]}` in a command). `reference_geometry` gives either as a line, a point as a line of no length, and `crossings` lays
them along the way the dimension measures (`measured_along`): a linear one's `orient` (horizontal or vertical), else square to its first line,
else from its first point to the next elsewhere. `Model::check` refuses a line not parallel to the first, or not square to a linear one's line,
and points all in one place. Mirror keeps the end of a line along the element and flips the one across it (`Reference::mirrored`); Flip swaps
both. A linear one given no `orient` runs vertical where `at` is east or west of everything it measures, else horizontal; the desktop's Auto
(`dims::Placing::kind`) also lays an aligned one where the cursor is among the points (`Orient::follow`), as Archicad does. Radial and diameter
dimensions measure round columns, curved walls (centre line or a face) and circles and arcs (`reference_arc`); arc length, a curved wall's or an
arc's length along it (`reference_sweep`), all of it or, with two point references after the arc, between them (`Model::arc_span`), its line an arc through `at` round the same centre. `dims::round_at` picks the face nearest a click.

Each dimension has a dimension type (`dims.rs`, `Model::dimension_types`, a library entry `Kind::DimensionType`, the `dimension_type` command),
Revit's type parameters with lengths in mm on paper: Dimension String Type (continuous, baseline, ordinate), tick mark (diagonal, arrow, open
arrow, dot, none) and its size, line and tick pens, colour, dimension line extension, Witness Line Control (gap to element, or fixed to the
dimension line with its length), witness line gap and extension, baseline spacing, centre marks, and its text: font (as text types take one,
`DimensionType::lettering`), size, bold, italic, underline, width factor, offset, opaque or transparent background, Read Convention, units and
rounding (`DimensionType::length`), and the radius and diameter symbols and the equality text. A project starts with `Diagonal - 2.5mm Arial`,
which aligned, linear, angular and arc length dimensions start in, and `Arrow - 2.5mm Arial`, which radial and diameter ones do
(`dims::default_type`); a file of format 9 gives its dimensions their kind's (`Model::typed_dimensions`). A dimension's own text, Revit's
instance values, is a prefix, a suffix, text above and below, Replace With Text and Equality Display, and a segment may have its own over it
(`texts`, `SegmentText`, the `dimension_text` command; `Dimension::text` reads one through the other, `dimension_segment_at` finds a segment by a
point); `Model::dimension_labels` is what its
numbers read (and `elements` shows as `labels`): a baseline string's each from its first reference, an ordinate's each witness line's, the first 0.
An aligned or linear dimension may be kept equal (`equal`, Revit's EQ, which also turns its Equality Display on) and have segments
locked at a length (`locked`, `Lock`; the `dimension_constraint` command). `constraints::keep` runs in `Session::execute` after every undoable
command, before the check: each constrained dimension is solved on its own line (its `stations`, each with its reference), a locked segment tying
two stations rigidly and equality tying all its segments to one length (a locked one's, else its ends', which stay where they are, so an inner
reference dragged goes back); a run of tied stations stays where what the command moved puts it, else where its first is. What has to move is
moved by `commands::move_by`, as `move` moves it, and the dimensions are solved again (`PASSES`) until all hold; where they can't (locked
lengths that differ made equal, one element pulled two ways), the command is refused, saying which dimension, and nothing changes.
A length typed for a segment (`dimension_value`; in the window, a click on the selected dimension's number, as a temporary
dimension's takes one) moves what the segment ends at, its second station's reference, along the dimension by the difference
(`move_by`), and a locked segment is locked at it; the other locks then hold or the command is refused. Align with `lock` (Revit's
padlock: in the window, the open padlock Align offers on the line it moved) leaves a lock: a dimension of the aligned line's reference
and the reference's (`to`, else whatever has a line along it), its one segment locked at 0 and `alignment` set, which
`constraints::keep` holds as it holds the others, so the two lines stay on one line whatever either is moved by; one that can't hold
with the other locks is refused, and the project is as it was. A lock is drawn by a front end, never on paper (`render/dimensions.rs`
draws nothing of it): the window shows each locked segment's shut padlock whether its dimension is selected or not, and each alignment
lock's padlock beside where its lines meet, which a click unlocks (deletes). Format 15 holds them; 14 would read one as a dimension of
nothing.
`render/dimensions.rs` draws them all as the type says (`Ink`: its lines, ticks and witness lines, and its numbers laid out by `crate::text`
over the paper where the background is opaque).

A 3D view has dimensions of its own (`Element::Dimension3D`, the `dimension_3d` command; `dims3d.rs`), as Revit's aligned dimension in a 3D
view: two references (`Ref3`), each a point of the model or a point on an edge (its two ends with it), and a point its line passes through,
kept by the view (`view`, a GUID: deleting the view takes them with it) and of a dimension type as a plan's are. Between two points it measures
straight from one to the other; to an edge, square to the edge's line, so between two parallel edges it is how far apart they are
(`dims3d::ends`). They hold places in space, not references to elements: moving an element leaves them, and `move`, `rotate` and `mirror`
take them in plan when they are moved themselves. They draw as marks (`dims3d::marks`, `Mark`: a polyline in the picture's pixels, its width
and colour), through any camera and at any paper size (`SCREEN` pixels a paper millimetre on screen, `sheet::DENSITY` on a sheet): a
witness line from each end of what it measures to its line, its line, a tick at each end and its number lettered along it in our strokes
(`font.rs`), reading from the left, on the side away from what it measures; nothing hides them. `dims3d::paint` paints marks into the
processor's picture, which the `render` command does for a 3D view; a sheet draws them as its own lines over the view's picture, so they print
in its PDF; the window draws them over the picture on either painter (the card's too) with the theme's ink, the selection's colour when
picked. Visibility/Graphics hides them with Dimensions (`category_of`). In the window the Aligned Dimension tool (DI) in the 3D view picks a
corner seen within the snap's reach (`Scene::corner_near`), else an edge within a pick's (`Scene::edge_near`, the point of it nearest the
cursor), else the point of the face there; after two, a click places the line where it meets the plane through the two that faces the
camera most (`dims3d::line_through`), and the status line says how long it is. In Modify a click on a dimension's lines picks it before what
the picture shows under them (`dims3d::pick`).

The sample house (cargo run --release -p bimcraft -- --sample): Revit's layout in BIMCraft's own icons and colours, with dimensions, door and window tags, a spot elevation, a note, a section and the four elevation marks, all built from BIMCraft commands. 207: them, walls joined at a corner stay joined when one moves, dimensions and tags follow what they measure and name, and 247:| Snaps and the ruler | Points picked while drawing stick to what the plan has there, as Revit's snaps do: the ends, middles and centres of walls (an arc's too), grids and components, the centres of columns, structural columns and footings with the corners and edge middles of their outlines (a round one's four quadrants), so a wall can start flush with a column's edge, and the corners of floors, ceilings, roofs and shafts; where two straight walls or grids cross; the foot of the perpendicular from the last point to a straight wall or grid; and a wall's centre line, so a wall drawn onto it meets it. It also sticks to the anchors of notes, dimensions, tags, spot elevations, section and elevation marks, detail groups and repeating details; a camera's mark gives its eye and target, never the body, lens or name it is drawn with. Each shows its own marker and its name. A direction from the last point sticks to multiples of an angle (5°, 15°, 30°, 45° or 90°; 15° by default), from east and from the line before it, so corners come out exact, sharp ones too: a dashed guide shows it, and where it crosses a wall or grid the point lands there. The line being drawn carries a ruler: graduations at round lengths, its length and its angle (at the corner it turns once there's a line before it, drawn as an arc). Manage > Snaps switches each snap and sets the angle steps, and Revit's SE, SM, SI, SC, SP and SN take one snap alone for the next point (SO none, SS back); Measure (ME) lays a ruler between two snapped points and reads its length, parts and angle; the `measure` command does the same. Each plan, section and elevation has a background grid, a main grid and a subgrid with their own spacing, divisions, colours and pens, turned by an angle, kept in the view's graphics and controlled by its template; Grid snapping (Manage > Snaps, or the grid menu in the view control bar) lands a free point on its crossings | 248:| Annotation | Aligned dimensions between parallel references, one segment or a chain: wall faces, centre lines and ends, door and window centres and jambs, grids; and between endpoints (a wall's ends and its faces' corners, a line's or a grid's ends, a jamb's), aligned along them or linear, horizontal or vertical, as the cursor lies or the Options Bar says (Auto, Aligned, Horizontal, Vertical; Space steps them); angular dimensions between two lines that meet, radial and diameter ones on round columns, curved walls, circles and arcs, and arc length ones along a curved wall or an arc; all measuring the model as it is, so they follow what they measure (a change that would turn a reference out of parallel with the others is refused). In a 3D view, aligned dimensions between two points or edges of the model (square to an edge), kept by the view and drawn over it, on either painter and on the sheets that hold it. A dimension's number takes a typed length and moves what it measures; locked segments show their padlocks always; Align leaves a padlock that keeps the two lines aligned after every change, refusing one the other locks can't hold with. Dimension types, as Revit's type parameters: continuous, baseline or ordinate strings, diagonal, arrow, open arrow or dot ticks, pens, colour, the dimension and witness lines' extensions, gaps and control, and the numbers' font, size, lettering, offset, background, read convention, units and rounding; a dimension's own prefix, suffix, text above and below, Replace With Text and Equality Display (EQ). Tags on any element showing its type, a door's or window's mark, a room's name or any field of its schedule, going where their doors and windows go, with or without a leader; tag everything not tagged yet in one go. Text notes in plans, sections, elevations and on sheets, at any angle, over several lines, with a leader, of a text type (font, size, bold, italic, underline, width factor, colour and a border: any font the system has, Arial by default, which a look-alike such as Liberation Sans stands in for where it isn't installed, or IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono or our single-stroke lettering; any script a font on the system has, CJK included), written and rewritten on the canvas (Shift+Enter breaks a line), and with Override Formatting, parts of them bold, italic or underlined whatever their type; spot elevations reading the top of what they stand on in plan (a floor, a roof's slope, a stair's tread), or the height of a point in a section | 249:| Views | A floor plan per level with Revit's view range: cut at its cut plane (1200 mm up by default), what lies below seen from it down to the bottom, faint beyond it down to the view depth, and roofs overhead up to the top: wall poché with clean joins at any angle, compound walls' layers, hatched with their materials' cut patterns where they're wide enough (else lighter where they aren't structure), door swings, window glass, room tags, grid bubbles, dimensions, door and window tags; PNG and SVG, which letter the view's name at the plan's bottom left (the window letters it too, over the canvas and on the screen only, which File > Settings can hide; a viewport on a sheet has its own title). Sections and elevations along any line: the cut in poché (a roof's along its slope, a compound wall's, floor's, roof's or ceiling's with its layers), what lies beyond in hidden line, levels named with their heights, grids; the four building elevations in one go; their marks on every plan; PNG. Crop regions on plans and sections: the view shows only what's inside, grids stopping at its edge with their bubbles. A reflected ceiling plan per level: its walls cut at 2300 mm (over the doors, through the windows), looking up at the ceilings, their tiles and the shafts through them, and at the beams and columns over the cut up to the ceilings, in projection (one over a ceiling is hidden by it). A 3D view, from any angle: walls with their doors and windows cut out, slabs and ceilings with their shafts cut out, columns, stairs and roofs, door leaves and glass, shaded (each layer in its material's colour), with an edge wherever faces meet, but none between the facets of a curve (a curved wall's, a round form's, an imported mesh's where its triangles turn less than 20°), which shades smoothly across them; PNG. A plan or a section always has a scale, 1 : n (1 : 100, or 1/8" = 1'-0" in feet and inches, until set): it stands for paper at that scale, and its annotation (lettering, grid bubbles, marks, dimension ticks) and its line weights are that paper's, so on screen a line is as thick as it would print at the zoom (at least a pixel; Thin Lines draws all of them one). A line weight is a pen, 1 to 16, or 0, a hairline, the thinnest line the screen, a PNG or a printer draws, at any scale and zoom; what pens 1 to 16 draw is the project's Line Weights (Manage > Line Weights, as Revit's): the model's pens at each of a list of scales, a view taking the nearest scale's, and the annotation's (dimensions, tags, text, grids, levels, marks) at any scale, edited by scale, added and deleted, applied as one undo step and saved with the project. Which pen each model category draws its own lines in, cut and seen, is the project's Object Styles (Manage > Object Styles, as Revit's), in every plan and section, a view's Visibility/Graphics over them. Detail lines draw in one view (a plan, a section, an elevation or a sheet) in a line style: a pen, a colour and a line pattern, its freely ordered gaps, straight strokes, dots, centered parallel offsets, waves, zigzags and text in mm on paper so it reads the same at any scale; the Line Pattern Creator previews straight or curved paths and letters text with bundled IBM Plex Sans, while geometry and dimensions keep the centerline (Manage > Line Styles, styles and patterns made, changed, renamed and deleted as one undo step; a project starts with Thin, Medium and Wide Lines, a Hairline, Hidden, Centre and Overhead Lines). A cut wall's outline is inked over its poché, and not across where walls join. A plan or a section has a detail level too: coarse (what it cuts in one poché, an opening as its gap and jambs), medium (a compound element's layers and an opening's leaf, swing and glass) or fine, as it has always drawn (the layers' patterns too); the 3D view has a visual style: shaded, hidden line (paper-white faces with their edges, what a face hides staying hidden) or wireframe (every edge, seen through the faces). A viewport takes its view's scale; a sheet keeps annotation at paper size. A view fitted into an image (a PNG, Zoom to Fit) leaves as much room round it as its annotation takes at its scale, which grows with the scale, so 1 : 500 doesn't cut its grid bubbles or level names off. A level can have more plans than its own, as Revit's Duplicate View makes them (`duplicate_view`, DP): each a plan view with its own view range, crop and graphics and its own dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations over the same model; with detailing it starts with its source's annotation; a dependent view follows its parent's view range and graphics (scale and detail too), has a crop of its own, and shows its parent's annotation as well as its own. They go on sheets, take view templates and have ceiling plans as levels do. Sections, elevations, schedules, sheets and the 3D view aren't duplicated yet. The 3D view is parallel (axonometric) or in perspective, as through a camera: picked from Projection in its Properties (or `perspective`), seen through a lens of a focal length typed there, from an eye raised or lowered to a height typed there, and orbited, panned, zoomed, picked and edited as ever, on the processor or the graphics card. The Camera tool (`camera`) makes a view of its own, as Revit's does: an eye and a target are clicked in a plan (each at a height over it, typed in the Options Bar), and a named 3D view in perspective opens looking from the eye at the target; it is listed under 3D Views in the Project Browser, opens from its own camera, and its name, eye, target and lens are read and changed in Properties, whether it is open or its mark on the plan is picked (`camera` reads or changes one too, by name or id; a view with no camera shows the azimuth and elevation it is framed by on a sheet instead). The camera shows on its level's plan as a mark at its eye with a line to what it looks at: it is picked there and opened by its right-click menu (or a double click), and its eye and target follow the mouse as the view is orbited, panned or zoomed, so leaving the view and coming back stands it where it was left. The 3D view has a section box, as Revit's: six planes square to the axes that keep what lies between them, the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, turned on and off with BX or its Properties, each face dragged by its grip in the view or typed in Properties, its extents kept while it's off; the levels it doesn't reach are left out. A plan can follow it (Section Box in the plan's Properties): it then shows what the box keeps, cut at the box's top, seen down to its bottom and cropped to its sides, and snaps to a scan where the box's top cuts it | 252:| Visibility and graphics | What each view hides, and how it draws the rest, as Revit's Visibility/Graphics does, for each plan, section, elevation and 3D view: whole categories left out (walls, doors, rooms, grids, dimensions, levels in a section…), or single elements; lines and fills overridden by category, by element and by view filter: a colour, weight and dash for what the view cuts and for what it sees (a plan's below its cut plane, the annotation; in 3D, and in a section beyond its line, the edges' colour), the cut's poché colour or a 3D view's surface colour (a weight is a pen, 0 a hairline at any scale), halftone (halfway to the paper) and, in 3D, transparency, where what lies behind shows through and a click still picks the element (halftone and transparency only add: a filter or an element can't take its category's away). A hidden door or window leaves its opening in the wall, and snaps, Tag All, Select All and a view's framing take what it shows. View filters pick elements out by rules, a schedule filter's (a field of the category, how to compare it, a value, project parameters among the fields), on the categories chosen; a view applies them in order, the first prevailing where they disagree, and one that hides hides whatever the others say; an element's own override beats the filters', and those beat the category's. View templates keep a view's categories, filters, phase, design options, scale, detail level, visual style and, for a plan, view range under a name, for other views to follow: what a template controls isn't the view's to change, and changed, every view following it follows. A project's filters and templates are saved with it; sheets print each view as its graphics say | 262:| Element ids | Every element, model or annotation, view, sheet or schedule, has an id, six digits from 100000 up, which commands, schedules and the desktop show and take, and a GUID, made once and never changed, as Revit's ElementId and UniqueId: what points at an element (a wall its level, a door its wall, a dimension what it measures, a viewport its view) holds its GUID, so an element that comes in from another file under a new id (Insert from File, `insert`; the same file inserted into itself is copied whole, each copy with a GUID of its own) breaks nothing. IFC writes each element's GUID as its GlobalId and reads it back as one; a file from before GUIDs opens with them, its ids moved up to six digits (1 is 100000). The library has them too: each type, material, picture, family, project parameter, view filter and template, phase, phase filter, design option set and design option has an id (counting down from 999999, so a new project's elements still start at 100000) and a GUID, kept through renames; in a file, whatever names one (a wall's type, a layer's material, a view's template, the phase an element is made in, its values of project parameters, keyed by the parameter's) holds its GUID, so renaming changes nothing in a file but the name. Commands take a library entry by its name or its GUID; `library` lists them, and Insert from File matches them by GUID, then by name. So do their parts: each type's layers and each family's forms and plan symbols hold an id and a GUID, kept while they stay where they are in their list (a type's layers given again, the Family Editor's forms moved), a copy getting its own; a family's types and parameters are library entries, so a component's type and its instance values (keyed by the parameter) are GUIDs in a file, and the materials a family's forms and parameters name too. Inside a family, its forms and types name its own parameters as its formulas do | 263:| Files | `.bimcraft` projects (JSON, file format 12: every save is 12, so an earlier build refuses even a plain project saved by this one, saying it is from a newer BIMCraft); IFC4 export with storeys, walls swept up from their plan outline (mitred where they join, an arc in short chords) or, attached to a roof, as closed shells, walls, floors, roofs and ceilings with their material layer sets (each material with its colour), slabs (sloped ones as closed shells), ceilings as coverings, spaces and columns, walls, slabs, doors and windows with their `Qto_*BaseQuantities` (a wall's side area and volume gross and less its openings, a slab's area and volume less its openings), beams (`IfcBeam`), footings (`IfcFooting`), pipes (`IfcPipeSegment`), conduits, cable trays and wires (`IfcCableCarrierSegment`, `IfcCableSegment`) and structural columns and floors, each along its own axis and, if structural, with `LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, the runs of a system assigned to an `IfcSystem` of its name, stairs and ramps as their flights, landings and railings (each railing with its rail's top line as its axis), roofs as closed shells of flat faces (hip, gable, shed or flat), openings that cut the walls and hold the doors and windows, an opening for each slab, ceiling and roof a shaft passes through, masses as building element proxies of object type `Mass` (a lofted one as a closed face set), and components as furniture, sanitary or waste terminals, pipe fittings, valves, distribution boards, outlets, switching devices, communications appliances, light fixtures or proxies, named `Family:Type` as Revit names them, each form a closed face set in its material's colour, each element's values of the project parameters in a `Project Parameters` property set (dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations belong to views, and stay out of it), and each element's phase and design option in a `BIMCraft_Phasing` property set: its `Phase Created` is always named in it, the first phase too (said to be implied, for another tool to read; a door or window says only what it holds, as one with no phase follows its wall), `Phase Demolished` and `Design Option` where it holds them, and the project's phases in order, with the phase filters, overrides and option sets it changed, in one on the project, and, as IFC says it, its `Status` in its `Pset_*Common` (`EXISTING`, `DEMOLISH`, `NEW` or `TEMPORARY`, for another tool to filter the work by); a project that uses none of it writes none | 265:| Desktop | Revit's layout: ribbon tabs with a contextual Modify tab, the Options Bar, Properties with the Type Selector and Type Properties, the Project Browser and views in tabs; a plan and a reflected ceiling plan per level that pan and zoom, sections and elevations, a 3D view that orbits, and sheets; tools for walls (straight or arcs, on the location line picked), doors, windows, columns, roofs by footprint (and Gable Edge, to stand a roof's edge upright) and by extrusion, dormers, floors (and a floor's slope arrow), ceilings, shaft openings, sketch mode (Edit Boundary on a floor, a ceiling, a roof or a shaft, and Boundary Line or Sketch Ceiling for a new one: lines, rectangles, arcs and Pick Walls, sketch lines with ids of their own picked by click or box and moved by their grips, Finish Edit Mode saying what's wrong and marking the lines; in the 3D view, Edit Boundary sketches on the element's own plane, and Floor, Ceiling, Roof and Shaft sketch on the view's Work Plane: a level from the list, a surface or three points picked on the model (snapping to corners), each with an offset, at any angle; walls, beams and braces, columns and structural columns, footings, pipes, ducts, conduits, cable trays and components draw in the 3D view on the level face under the cursor, snapping as a plan does, a run climbing from one face to another; they need it horizontal), masses (and floors, walls and roofs from them), stairs and ramps (run by run, turning at landings), railings, rooms, levels, grids, dimensions (aligned, angular, radial), spot elevations, text, detail lines, filled and masking regions, tags, sections and elevations; Flip, Attach Top/Base and Detach Top/Base for walls; a wall, floor, roof or ceiling type's layers in Type Properties, and the project's materials in Manage > Materials; project parameters in Manage > Project Parameters, and their values in Properties; schedules from View > Schedules, their fields, filters, sorting and totals in Schedule Properties; the Component tool, families and their types in the Type Selector, the Project Browser and Type Properties, a component's own parameters in Properties, and Load Family; Crop View with grips to drag a crop region's edges, and the view range in Properties; project units, metric or feet and inches; Revit's selection (click, Ctrl, Shift, Tab, window and crossing boxes); dragging and the Modify panel (Align, Offset, Mirror, Split, Move, Copy, Rotate, Trim/Extend to Corner) and its Phasing panel (Demolish); Paint and Remove Paint on its Geometry panel, for the 3D view; typed lengths and temporary dimensions; undo and redo; open, save and export; a light and a dark theme; English, Portuguese or Spanish. The Manage tab has the Materials window (with textures and pictures), the Favorites, Object Styles, Annotation Settings (Line Weights, Line Styles, Line Patterns and Fill Patterns, a fill pattern simple or made of detail lines picked in a plan and the tile between two corners), and the Family Editor (New Family, Edit Family) | 304: 377:| Dimension, tag | Annotate > Aligned (DI): pick parallel references, each the line nearest the cursor (a wall's face, centre line or end, a door's or window's centre or jamb, a grid), or endpoints (a wall's end or corner, a line's or a grid's end), which a square marks, then click away from them where the dimension line goes; more picks make a chain. Linear: pick endpoints, then click where it goes, horizontal or vertical as the cursor lies; the Options Bar's Place (Auto, Aligned, Horizontal, Vertical; Space steps them) lays either tool's dimension. Angular: pick two lines that meet, then click where the arc goes; the angle on that side. Radial and Diameter: pick a round column, a curved wall, a circle or an arc, then click where it goes. Arc Length: pick a curved wall or an arc, then, to measure part of it, two ends on it, then click where the dimension's arc goes. Edit Type on a dimension opens Dimension Type Properties; a double click on one of its numbers opens Dimension Text, that segment's own prefix, suffix, text above and below, or text in its place. Selected, a dimension shows a padlock under each segment and EQ past its end: a click locks a segment at its length, or keeps the segments equal, and what it measures to then moves with what moves, as in Revit. Click it again, and it comes back. A door or window with no phase of its own comes down with its wall without being touched, and a click on it says so; something that holds no parameters, such as a dimension, says so and stays as it was. The tool stays on until Esc | 389:| Lengths | While a tool waits for its next point, type a length and press Enter: it goes that far toward the cursor. content.content:
A level's own plan is the level (its `view_range`, `crop` and `graphics` are the level's); every other plan of it is an `Element::PlanView`
(Revit's Duplicate View: `duplicate_view`, which only plans take). A plan has a key: the level's id, or a plan view's. `Model::plan_level` says
which level a key shows, and everything that draws or measures the model takes that level (`draw_plan`, `plan_shows`, the canvas's tools), while
what is the view's own takes the key: its graphics (`graphics_of`), view range (`view_range_of`, which a template may control), crop (`crop_of`)
and annotation. Annotation says which view it is in: a note or a spot elevation by `view`, a dimension or a tag by an optional `view` beside its
`level` or its host (none: the level's own plan), and `Model::annotation_in` asks whether a plan draws it. A command that takes a `level` takes a
plan view too (`plan_param`): what is built stands on its level, what is dimensioned or tagged is in the view. A dependent view (`parent`) follows
its parent's view range and graphics (`plan_source`; `graphics`, `scale`, `detail` and `visual_style` refuse it, naming the parent), has a crop
of its own and draws its parent's annotation as well as its own. Deleting a view deletes what is annotated in it and its dependents; a level
takes its plan views with it. A project that has none writes the same file as before. A plan's own name, lettered at its bottom left, is in the drawings that make an image (`plan`, `ceiling_plan`: `titled`), not in the window's (`draw`, `draw_ceiling`) or a sheet's (`draw_at`), where the tab and the viewport's title say it. The desktop: View > Duplicate View, DP, and the Project
Browser's right-click, which also has Delete for a plan view; `Sheet::Plan` and `Sheet::Ceiling` hold the key.

content.content:
undo | Undo | {count?} takes back the last `count` steps (1 by default)

redo | Redo | {count?} does again the last `count` steps undone (1 by default)

level | Level | {elevation, name?, extent?: [[x,y],[x,y]]} a level at an elevation in mm; `extent`, the rectangle in plan its plane stretches over (south-west corner, then north-east), where sections, elevations and the 3D view show it (without one, the model's, a metre past it)

grid | Grid | {start: [x,y], end: [x,y], name?} names follow the last grid: 1, 2… or A, B…

wall | Wall | {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, arc?, location?, attach_top?, attach_base?, room_bounding?} one wall per segment of its location line; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall (unconnected), or up to `top_level`, `top_offset` mm above it (0; negative, below it; the top must stay above the base). `arc`: degrees each turns from its start to its end, counter-clockwise (180, a half circle bulging to its right). `location`: the line of it the points are on: centre (the default), core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core or interior-core; its exterior side is to the left of its start to its end, so walls drawn clockwise face out. `attach_top`, `attach_base`: a roof or floor its top follows from below, or its base stands on. `room_bounding`: false for a wall rooms run past (a low wall, a balustrade); true, the default, bounds them

door | Door | {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?, flip_hand?} in the wall under `at`, or in `wall` centred `offset` mm from its start; with `family`, a door family's `type` (its first by default), which sizes the opening and draws the door

window | Window | {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, sill?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?} like door; `sill` defaults to the type's (a family's `Sill Height`)

column | Column | {at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column, its width along `angle` degrees; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`

structural_column | Structural Column | {at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column of the structure, as `column` makes one but in its own category with its own types (`type` with category structural column): up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`. CL is `column`'s too; on the desktop's Structure tab it is this one

duplicate_view | Duplicate View | {view, mode?: duplicate|detailing|dependent, name?} a new plan view of a plan's level (a level's own plan, or a plan view; sections, elevations, schedules, sheets and the 3D view aren't duplicated yet): `duplicate` (the default) has the same view range, crop and graphics and no annotation of its own; `detailing` copies the dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations in it too, as its own; `dependent` follows its parent's view range, graphics, scale and detail (change those in the parent), has a crop of its own and shows its parent's annotation as well as its own. Named `name`, else `<view> Copy 1` (`<view> Dependent 1`). Commands that take a level or a view take it by name or id, and what is drawn, dimensioned, tagged or noted there is in it

flip | Flip | {ids: [wall,…]} turns walls round about their location lines, as Revit's flip arrows do: their exterior sides go to the other side, their doors and windows stay where they are

modify | Modify | {id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); to put a pattern line of one on a reference line, Model::align_pattern gives the `pattern_origin` that does. A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it

copy | Copy | {ids: [id,…], by: [dx, dy]} copies elements, with the doors and windows of copied walls; returns the copies' ids

rotate | Rotate | {ids: [id,…], about: [x, y], angle, copy?} turns elements about a point by `angle` degrees, counter-clockwise; walls joined to them stay joined, and doors and windows turn with their walls

mirror | Mirror | {ids: [id,…], axis: [[x, y], [x, y]], copy?} mirrors elements across the line through two points; mirrored doors and windows face the other way

corner | Trim/Extend to Corner | {ids: [a, b], keep?: [[x, y], [x, y]]} trims or extends two walls, or two detail lines (lines or arcs), to meet where their lines (or circles) cross; `keep` is a point on the part of each to keep

offset | Offset | {id, distance, toward: [x, y], copy?} a detail line drawn again `distance` mm beside itself on the side `toward` is, arcs round the same centres, an ellipse or a spline as a spline through points within 0.05 mm of the true offset (which Revit can't): a copy (the default), or with `copy` false moved

trim_extend | Trim/Extend Single Element | {boundary, ids: [id, …], keep: [[x, y], …]} trims or extends each detail line of `ids` (lines and arcs) to where it meets `boundary` (a detail line, a wall's location line or a grid), keeping the part of each its `keep` point is on: Revit's Trim/Extend Single Element, and Multiple Elements with several

split | Split | {id, at: [x, y]} splits a wall or a detail line in two at `at`: a wall's doors and windows go with their part; a detail line of any shape splits where it passes nearest `at` (a spline by its control points exactly, one through points into two through points within 0.05 mm of it), and a closed one (a circle, a whole ellipse, a closed polyline) opens there instead, into one that starts and ends at `at`

join_polyline | Join into Polyline | {ids: [id, …]} joins detail lines of one view, lines, arcs and polylines that meet end to end, into one polyline in the first's line style (closed when they come round); the first keeps its id, the rest are deleted, and a dimension that measured one of the rest loses that reference (and is deleted, left with fewer than two): the reply's `notes` say which

vertex | Add/Delete Vertex | {id, at: [x, y], delete?} a detail line (a polyline, or a spline of either kind) with a vertex more where it passes nearest `at` (a spline by its control points gains a control point and keeps its shape exactly), or with `delete` one fewer: the corner, control point or point passed through nearest `at`; `at` is within 100 mm of the line (of a vertex, to delete one), or it is refused

explode | Explode Polyline | {id} takes a detail line that is a polyline apart into a line or an arc for each segment, in its view and style; the first keeps its id. Revit has no shortcut for it: EX is ours, PX being the Plumbing Fixture's on the desktop

delete | Delete | {ids: [id,…]} deleting a wall deletes its doors and windows, deleting those their tags; a view takes its notes and spot elevations, and what a spot elevation reads takes it; dimensions lose what's deleted

detail_line | Detail Line | {view?, style?, and a curve: `points` [[x, y], …] (with `arcs`, each segment's turn in degrees counter-clockwise, and `closed`), `start` and `end` (with `arc` degrees or a `through` point), `centre` and `radius` (a circle), `centre` and `radii` [a, b] (an ellipse, with `angle` degrees and `span` [from, to] degrees for part of one), `control` [[x, y], …] (a spline by its control points, with `knots`), or `fit` [[x, y], …] (a spline through them, with `start_tangent` and `end_tangent`)} a detail line in a view, by name or id, in the view's own terms: a level's plan (the lowest by default; plan mm), a section or an elevation (along its line from its start, and up) or a sheet by number (paper mm). It draws in line style `style` (Thin Lines unless told), only in its view, and goes with it; with `insulation`, a width in mm, it draws as batt insulation along its curve, as Revit's Insulation; with `centre_mark` true, a small cross marks the centre of its arcs, circle or ellipse; with `cloud`, an arc length in mm, it draws as a revision cloud's scallops along it (outward round a loop, a scallop ending at each corner), of `revision` (any text, a label kept with the cloud and listed by `elements`; nothing else reads it); a line is insulation or a cloud, not both. An arc, a circle or an ellipse lies within 1,000 km of the origin (an arc of 359.9999999999° is a circle of radius 5.7e14 mm, and is refused), and a polyline's arcs take no more than 8,192 points to draw within 0.25 mm: 10,000 arcs of 175° are refused

elements | Elements | {category?, level?, limit?, offset?} elements with their `id` (six digits, what commands take) and `guid` (made once, never changed), fields and derived values (length, height, area_m2…); what an element points at (its level, host, view…) it holds by GUID. Wherever a command takes an element, its id or its GUID will do

a plan cuts (`Model::bounding`). In a section or an elevation, points run along its line from its start, and up; on a sheet,
they're paper mm from its bottom left corner; notes and spot elevations live in those terms in their view.
A wall's `start` and `end` are on its location line: its centre line unless `location` says otherwise (`walls::faces`).
Its exterior is to the left of start to end, as in Revit, so walls drawn clockwise face out; a compound type lists its
layers from the exterior in, and a floor, roof or ceiling type from the top down (IFC import turns a wall round, or a slab's
layers over, by the way its layer set's usage stacks them). A layer's material is a name in the project's library
(`Model::materials`): its colour shades the layer in 3D, its cut pattern is a drafting pattern (`GAP` px apart on screen and
paper, where the layer is `PATTERN_ROOM` px wide), its surface pattern a model pattern (`MODULE` mm, its real size). A curved wall turns `arc` degrees, counter-clockwise positive (`walls::Axis`). Where walls meet,
their faces meet in mitred caps at any angle, and a wall ending on another stops at its face (`walls::cap`); plans, 3D,
sections and IFC all draw that outline (`walls::outline`, `walls::prisms`). Room areas are measured at the walls' centre
lines, run on or back to meet at joins (`walls::centre_line`). A room separator (`roomseparator`, made by `room_separator` a line per segment) bounds rooms as a wall's centre line
would and nothing else: it is no edge of a floor, a ceiling or a roof (`Model::bounding_lines` takes it, `wall_lines` and
`face_lines` don't; an end drawn to a wall's face runs on to its centre line there, so the line splits rooms measured at
the centre lines too), it is drawn in plan only, and it goes to IFC as an `IfcVirtualElement` of `ObjectType` `RoomSeparation`
with an `Axis` polyline on its storey, which the import reads back. The desktop's Room Separator, beside Room, lays one a
click from the point before until Esc. A room's height is Revit's: from `base_offset` over its level up to `limit_offset` over
its Upper Limit, `top_level` (none: Not Bounded, the offset then over its own level). A new room reaches 300 mm under the
level above (`ROOM_BELOW_ABOVE`), or with none above is Not Bounded and 2500 mm tall; a room read from a file without them is
Not Bounded, 2500 mm. `Model::room_span` and `room_height` give it, `elements` its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3` (the area times that height, not cut by floors or roofs), and the IFC
space is swept that tall. A room's colour on plans (`Room::colour`) styles that solid in IFC as other elements' colours do: an
`IfcStyledItem` on the swept solid, its unnamed `IfcSurfaceStyle` shading in the colour (`IfcSurfaceStyleShading`, which IFC4's
rendering style extends; `Step::surface_style`, which a material's style shares), so a viewer shades the space in it. The import
reads it back from the colour the space's body is styled in (`import::item_colours`), so a round trip keeps it and a space
another program styled comes in filled in its colour; a room that isn't enclosed has no body, so no colour, in IFC. A frozen room (`frozen`, an instance parameter: `room {frozen}` or `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the

import subprocess, json, os, tempfile, shutil, sys
exe = '/workspace/executable'
L = float(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 10000.0
def parallel(dy):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(dir='/tmp/views-dims')
    cmds = ['detail_line {"start":[0,0],"end":[%r,0]}' % L,
            'detail_line {"start":[0,1000],"end":[%r,%r]}' % (L, 1000 + dy),
            'dimension {"refs":[{"id":100002},{"id":100003}],"at":[5000,500]}']
    args = [exe, 'run']
    for c in cmds: args += ['--cmd', c]
    p = subprocess.run(args, cwd=d, capture_output=True)
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return b'values' in p.stdout.split(b'\n')[-2]
lo, hi = L * 0.0009, L * 0.0011
for i in range(40):
    m = (lo + hi) / 2
    if parallel(m): lo = m
    else: hi = m

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""labels.py [-m] 'setup;;cmds' v1 v2 ... : prints the label of a dimension of each length v_i
(between a detail line at y=0 and one at y=v_i), after the setup commands."""
import subprocess, json, os, tempfile, shutil, sys
exe = '/workspace/executable'
a = sys.argv[1:]
if a[0] == '-m':
    exe = os.environ['MINE']; a = a[1:]
setup = [c for c in a[0].split(';;') if c.strip()]
vals = [float(x) for x in a[1:]]
d = tempfile.mkdtemp(dir='/tmp/views-dims')
cmds = list(setup) + ['detail_line {"start":[0,0],"end":[1000,0]}']
for v in vals:
    cmds.append('detail_line {"start":[0,%r],"end":[1000,%r]}' % (v, v))
args = [exe, 'run']
for c in cmds: args += ['--cmd', c]
args += ['--save', 'x.bimcraft']
p = subprocess.run(args, cwd=d, capture_output=True)
pr = json.load(open(os.path.join(d, 'x.bimcraft')))
ids = sorted(int(k) for k, e in pr['elements'].items() if e['category'] == 'line')
base = ids[0]
args = [exe, 'run', 'x.bimcraft']
for i in ids[1:]:
    args += ['--cmd', 'dimension {"refs":[{"id":%d},{"id":%d}],"at":[500,-1]}' % (base, i)]
args += ['--cmd', 'elements {"category":"dimension"}']
p = subprocess.run(args, cwd=d, capture_output=True)
shutil.rmtree(d)
out = p.stdout.decode().strip().split('\n')[-1]
try:
    els = json.loads(out)['elements']
    for v, e in zip(vals, els):
        print(repr(v), e['values'], e['labels'])
except Exception:
    print(p.stdout.decode(), p.stderr.decode())

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""bisect_join.py L|T lo hi [type]: find the join tolerance.
L: wall A (0,0)-(5000,0), wall B starting at (5000+g, 0) going north; joined if A's left end x != 5000.
T: wall A (0,0)-(5000,0), wall B starting at (2000, g) going north; joined if B's right start y == 100 (face)."""
import subprocess, json, os, tempfile, shutil, sys
exe = '/workspace/executable'
mode, lo, hi = sys.argv[1], float(sys.argv[2]), float(sys.argv[3])
typ = sys.argv[4] if len(sys.argv) > 4 else None
def val(cmds):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(dir='/tmp/views-dims')
    args = [exe, 'run']
    for c in cmds: args += ['--cmd', c]
    p = subprocess.run(args, cwd=d, capture_output=True)
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return json.loads(p.stdout.decode().strip().split('\n')[-1])['values'][0]
def joined(g):
    t = (',"type":"%s"' % typ) if typ else ''
    if mode == 'L':
        cmds = ['wall {"points":[[0,0],[5000,0]]%s}' % t, 'wall {"points":[[%r,0],[%r,4000]]}' % (5000 + g, 5000 + g),
                'grid {"start":[-50000,-100000],"end":[-50000,100000]}',
                'dimension {"refs":[{"id":100004},{"id":100002,"face":"left","point":"end"}],"at":[-60000,0]}']
        v = val(cmds) - 50000
        return abs(v - 5000) > 1e-6
    else:
        cmds = ['wall {"points":[[0,0],[5000,0]]%s}' % t, 'wall {"points":[[2000,%r],[2000,4000]]}' % g,
                'grid {"start":[-100000,-50000],"end":[100000,-50000]}',
                'dimension {"refs":[{"id":100004},{"id":100003,"face":"right","point":"start"}],"at":[0,-60000]}']
        v = val(cmds) - 50000
        return abs(v - g) > 1e-6
for i in range(30):
    m = (lo + hi) / 2
    if joined(m): lo = m
    else: hi = m
print(mode, typ, 'joined up to', lo, 'not at', hi)

"""bisect_join2.py lo hi through_type t_type [angle_deg]: T tolerance with given types; B starts at (2000, g)
going in direction angle (90 = north)."""
import subprocess, json, os, tempfile, shutil, sys, math
exe = '/workspace/executable'
lo, hi = float(sys.argv[1]), float(sys.argv[2])
ta, tb = sys.argv[3], sys.argv[4]

    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(dir='/tmp/views-dims')
    args = [exe, 'run']
    for c in cmds: args += ['--cmd', c]
    p = subprocess.run(args, cwd=d, capture_output=True)
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return json.loads(p.stdout.decode().strip().split('\n')[-1])['values'][0]
def joined(g):
    ex, ey = 2000 + 4000 * math.cos(math.radians(ang)), g + 4000 * math.sin(math.radians(ang))
    cmds = ['wall {"points":[[0,0],[5000,0]],"type":"%s"}' % ta, 'wall {"points":[[2000,%r],[%r,%r]],"type":"%s"}' % (g, ex, ey, tb),

            'dimension {"refs":[{"id":100004},{"id":100003,"face":"right","point":"start"}],"at":[0,-60000]}']
    v = val(cmds) - 50000
    return abs(v - g) > 1e-6
for i in range(30):
    m = (lo + hi) / 2
    if joined(m): lo = m
    else: hi = m
print(ta, tb, ang, 'joined up to', round(lo, 6))

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""randjoin.py seed n: builds a random wall layout with the original and compares every wall's
face and end points between the two programs."""
import subprocess, json, os, sys, random, tempfile, shutil
seed = int(sys.argv[1]); n = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 4
random.seed(seed)
types = ['Generic - 200mm', 'Exterior - 300mm', 'Interior - 100mm']
locs = ['centre', 'exterior-finish', 'interior-finish', 'core-centre', 'exterior-core', 'interior-core']
cmds = []
def pt():
    return [random.randint(-8, 8) * 500, random.randint(-8, 8) * 500]
for k in range(n):
    kind = random.random()
    t = random.choice(types)
    extra = ''
    if random.random() < 0.3:
        extra += ',"location":"%s"' % random.choice(locs)
    if kind < 0.5:
        # a polyline, closed or not
        m = random.randint(2, 4)
        pts = [pt() for _ in range(m)]
        closed = 'true' if (m >= 3 and random.random() < 0.5) else 'false'
        cmds.append('wall {"points":%s,"closed":%s,"type":"%s"%s}' % (json.dumps(pts), closed, t, extra))
    else:
        cmds.append('wall {"points":%s,"type":"%s"%s}' % (json.dumps([pt(), pt()]), t, extra))
d = tempfile.mkdtemp(dir='/tmp/views-dims')
args = ['/workspace/executable', 'run']
for c in cmds:
    args += ['--cmd', c]
args += ['--cmd', 'grid {"start":[-100000,-50000],"end":[100000,-50000]}', '--cmd', 'grid {"start":[-50000,-100000],"end":[-50000,100000]}', '--save', 'r.bimcraft']
p = subprocess.run(args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, text=True)
if not os.path.exists(os.path.join(d, 'r.bimcraft')):
    print('build failed', p.stderr.strip()[:200]); sys.exit(0)
pr = json.load(open(os.path.join(d, 'r.bimcraft')))
proj = '/tmp/views-dims/rand%d.bimcraft' % seed
shutil.copy(os.path.join(d, 'r.bimcraft'), proj)
shutil.rmtree(d)
walls = [k for k, e in pr['elements'].items() if e['category'] == 'wall']
grids = [k for k, e in pr['elements'].items() if e['category'] == 'grid']
refs = []
for w in walls:
    for face in ['centre', 'left', 'right', 'start', 'end']:
        for point in ['start', 'end']:
            refs.append('{"id":%s,"face":"%s","point":"%s"}' % (w, face, point))
out = subprocess.run(['python3', '/tmp/views-dims/ptcmp.py', proj, grids[0], grids[1]] + refs, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
print('seed', seed, out.strip().split('\n')[-1])
if 'same' in out and out.strip().split('\n')[-1].split('/')[0] != out.strip().split('\n')[-1].split('/')[1].split(' ')[0]:
    print('\n'.join(cmds))
    print(out)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""bisect_sharp.py t1 t2: the angle (degrees, between the two walls' ways out of their joint)
below which their corner is squared off instead of mitred."""
import subprocess, json, os, tempfile, shutil, sys, math
exe = '/workspace/executable'
ta = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 'Generic - 200mm'
tb = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 'Generic - 200mm'
def mitred(ang):
    # wall A from (5000,0) to the joint (0,0); wall B from the joint out at `ang` degrees from A's way back
    a = math.radians(ang)
    bx, by = 5000 * math.cos(a), 5000 * math.sin(a)
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(dir='/tmp/views-dims')
    cmds = ['wall {"points":[[5000,0],[0,0]],"type":"%s"}' % ta, 'wall {"points":[[0,0],[%r,%r]],"type":"%s"}' % (bx, by, tb),
            'grid {"start":[-50000,-100000],"end":[-50000,100000]}',
            'dimension {"refs":[{"id":100004},{"id":100002,"face":"left","point":"end"}],"at":[-60000,0]}']
    args = [exe, 'run']
    for c in cmds: args += ['--cmd', c]
    p = subprocess.run(args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, text=True)
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    v = json.loads(p.stdout.strip().split('\n')[-1])['values'][0] - 50000
    return abs(v) > 0.01   # A's left face end not at x=0 means it was mitred
lo, hi = 0.5, 90.0
print('at 60', mitred(60), 'at 5', mitred(5))
for i in range(30):
    m = (lo + hi) / 2
    if mitred(m): hi = m
    else: lo = m
print(ta, tb, 'squared below', lo, 'mitred above', hi)
